summary: Leviticus 18 addresses Israel as a people leaving Egypt for Canaan and commands them to follow Yahweh’s statutes rather than surrounding practices. It prohibits sexual access to close relatives and also names adultery, sex during menstrual uncleanness, child sacrifice to Molech, male-male intercourse, and sex with animals. The conclusion includes both Israelites and resident foreigners, links these acts to defiling the land, and warns that offenders will be cut off.
whyItMatters: The speech joins kinship, sexual conduct, worship, and continued life in the land. Its warning also places Israel under the same possibility of expulsion that it attributes to the land’s previous inhabitants.

context.author: The text presents this instruction as Yahweh’s word through Moses; authorship and final composition are debated
context.audience: The children of Israel, with resident foreigners among them included in the concluding prohibition
context.date: The speech places Israel between life in Egypt and entry into Canaan; the date of final composition is debated
context.setting: Israel’s wilderness journey toward Canaan, framed by covenant loyalty and life in the land
context.literaryForm: Covenant law governing kinship, sexual conduct, worship, and land defilement

outline.heading: Yahweh’s statutes instead of Egypt’s and Canaan’s
outline.note: The law begins with covenant identity, a rejection of surrounding statutes, and the promise of life in God’s ordinances.

outline.heading: Boundaries around close relatives
outline.note: A general ban on uncovering a close relative’s nakedness is specified across parents, siblings, descendants, aunts, in-laws, and linked women.

outline.heading: Menstrual uncleanness and adultery
outline.note: The next commands prohibit sexual approach during menstrual impurity and intercourse with a neighbor’s wife.

outline.heading: Molech sacrifice, male-male intercourse, and animals
outline.note: Child sacrifice profanes God’s name, while the following commands prohibit specified sexual acts.

outline.heading: Land defilement and the sanction of being cut off
outline.note: Israelite and resident foreigner are warned not to repeat practices associated with the land’s former inhabitants.

keyVerses.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances, which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: God’s statutes, rather than surrounding practices, are presented as the way of life for Israel.

keyVerses.text: “‘You shall not lie with a man as with a woman. That is detestable.
keyVerses.why: The chapter states its prohibition of the named male-male sexual act directly.

keyVerses.text: that the land not vomit you out also, when you defile it, as it vomited out the nation that was before you.
keyVerses.why: The expulsion warning applies to Israel as well as the land’s earlier inhabitants.

questions.question: What is the chapter’s historical and covenant setting?
questions.answer: Yahweh addresses the children of Israel as people who lived in Egypt and are being brought to Canaan. They are commanded not to imitate either land’s statutes but to walk in his; the closing rule also includes foreigners residing within Israel’s land community.

questions.question: What does “uncover their nakedness” mean in the kinship list?
questions.answer: It is the chapter’s repeated expression for forbidden sexual access, as the parallel commands to approach, take, or lie with someone make clear. The phrase organizes relationships by family connection rather than inviting a merely literal reading about accidental nudity.

questions.question: Why does the law list so many different relatives?
questions.answer: After the general close-relative ban, the text maps it through parents and their spouses, siblings and half-siblings, grandchildren, aunts, daughters-in-law, a brother’s wife, and a woman with her descendants. The specificity applies the general rule across kinship created through birth and marriage.

questions.question: Does verse 19 make menstruation a moral offense?
questions.answer: The verse forbids sexual approach during the woman’s menstrual impurity. It treats intercourse during that status as prohibited conduct; menstruation itself is not called an offense.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about Molech?
questions.answer: It prohibits giving any of one’s children as a sacrifice to Molech and says doing so profanes God’s name. This chapter does not supply Molech’s history or ritual details, so its own clear claim is the rejection of child sacrifice as rival worship.

questions.question: What precisely does verse 22 prohibit?
questions.answer: The WEB prohibits a man from lying “with a man as with a woman” and calls the act detestable. The command belongs to this ancient Israelite account of prohibited sexual conduct; it does not define modern categories of sexual orientation or civil marriage. Its ancient legal wording and later interpretations are distinct questions.

questions.question: Why are the prohibitions about animals placed here?
questions.answer: Verse 23 prohibits both a man and a woman from sexual union with an animal and describes the acts as defiling and a perversion. The placement continues the chapter’s sequence of prohibited sexual boundaries, but the text gives no further theory of why the items appear in this exact order.

questions.question: What does it mean that the land “vomited out” its inhabitants?
questions.answer: The speech pictures the land expelling inhabitants because of the listed practices and warns Israel of the same outcome. God’s giving the land does not make Israel exempt from the chapter’s conditions for remaining in it.

questions.question: What consequences and scope does the conclusion give these rules?
questions.answer: Verse 29 says those who commit the listed acts will be “cut off from among their people.” The surrounding verses also threaten expulsion from the land, and the command applies to native-born and resident foreigner alike. This chapter gives no procedure for carrying out the cutting-off sanction.

glossary.def: The chapter’s recurring expression for forbidden sexual access within specified relationships.
The named recipient of the child sacrifice forbidden in verse 21; this chapter gives no fuller identification.
The severe covenant sanction stated in verse 29, whose mechanism is not defined in this chapter.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The preceding speech directs offerings to the Tent and forbids eating blood, applying several rules to Israelites and resident foreigners alike. The next set of commands addresses family relationships, sex, and worship.

here.text: Israel is told to follow God’s statutes as it moves from Egypt toward Canaan. The prohibitions are followed by warnings about defilement, expulsion from the land, and being cut off.

after.text: Chapter 19 addresses the whole congregation with a call to holiness that joins worship to harvest sharing, wages, justice, neighbor-love, and treatment of resident foreigners.
